sections.title: Short and long pairs
sections.content: Hungarian vowels come in seven short/long pairs — *á*, *é*, *í*, *ó*, *ő*, *ú* and *ű* are not decoration but distinct sounds. For five of the pairs (*i*/*í*, *o*/*ó*, *ö*/*ő*, *u*/*ú*, *ü*/*ű*) the long version is just held longer, same sound. Two of them, *a*/*á* and *e*/*é*, also change quality: *a* is like British "hot", *á* is like "father"; *e* is like "bet", *é* is a purer, longer "ay" with no glide. And *ö*/*ő* and *ü*/*ű* don't exist in English at all: round your lips as if to say "oh" or "oo", but say "eh" or "ee" instead.

Those accent marks aren't decoration — *kor* ("age") and *kór* ("illness") are different words. Hungarians hear vowel length the way English speakers hear the difference between "bit" and "beat." Treat every *á*/*é*/*í*/*ó*/*ő*/*ú*/*ű* as its own letter, not a typo waiting to be ignored.
The example words above are real human recordings, not synthetic speech — sourced from Wikimedia Commons (recorded by contributor Panda10, licensed CC BY-SA).
